levels.label: Extreme
regions: Persian Gulf and Permian Basin industrial flare fields
Active volcanic belts (Pacific Ring of Fire)
causes: High-intensity crown fires running through dense forest fuel ladders
Severe pyrocumulonimbus-generating conflagrations under dry gusting winds
High-throughput upstream petroleum and gas production flare stacks
Active subaerial volcanic lava vents and pyroclastic fountaining
issues: Stratospheric smoke injection punching through the tropopause
Severe soil heating that can consume deep organic layers and seed banks
Extreme radiant heat fluxes preventing direct wildland attack
Long-range transboundary transport of toxic atmospheric aerosols

air_climate: Violent pyroconvection can inject black carbon and reactive aerosol plumes directly into the stratosphere, where they can persist for months and perturb regional albedo.
Massive short-term pulses of greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) commonly accelerate atmospheric warming.
Industrial flaring can emit concentrated sulfur dioxide (SO2) contributing to localized acid precipitation, alongside elevated NOx forming ground-level ozone.
soil_land: Extreme heat commonly sterilizes upper soil layers, eliminating mycorrhizal fungal networks and beneficial microbial communities.
Severe burn severity can vaporize soil organic compounds that condense into a subsurface hydrophobic (water-repellent) crust, sharply elevating landslide and catastrophic post-fire debris flow risks.
Unenclosed industrial flares may deposit heavy metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) onto surrounding soil.
water: Post-fire storms can wash massive loads of ash, toxic heavy metals, and particulate sediment into drinking water catchments and reservoirs.
Excessive nutrient runoff (phosphorus, nitrogen) can trigger rapid eutrophication and toxic cyanobacterial blooms, causing widespread fish kills.
Hydrocarbon breakdown products such as benzene can potentially leach into municipal drinking water conduits following severe soil heating.
snow_ice: Refractory black carbon particles can settle onto sub-Arctic snowpack and alpine glaciers, lowering surface albedo and accelerating seasonal melt cycles.
Soot deposition on snow surfaces can advance snow-cover depletion by several weeks, triggering early streamflow depletion.
wildlife: Stand-replacing thermal intensity can destroy critical nesting trees, old-growth snags, and sub-canopy microclimates.
Severe burns may facilitate the rapid colonisation of fire-prone invasive cheatgrass and flammable shrub species, altering natural succession.
Intense luminescent radiance from continuous high-volume flares can disrupt migratory bird navigation and nocturnal insect feeding behaviour.
human_health: Extreme PM2.5 concentrations exceeding hundreds of micrograms per cubic metre can cause acute cardiovascular crises, severe asthma exacerbations, and premature mortality.
Volatile organic compounds, benzene, and formaldehyde from unburned flare gases can elevate occupational cancer hazards and chronic respiratory disease.
Catastrophic wildland fire runs may destroy community infrastructure, municipal drinking water grids, and timber reserves.

response_options: Stationary hotspots: Flare gas recovery units (FGRU) and enclosed combustors represent proven engineering methods to capture waste gas, mitigating methane and volatile organic emissions.

Stationary heat recovery: Industrial literature cites Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) power generators for converting high-temperature industrial heat (reported range 1 to 150+ MW electricity, unverified working assumption from technical literature; radiative power seen from space is not recoverable energy).

Wildland zones: Mechanical fuel thinning, defensible fuel profile zones (DFPZs), and rapid hydromulching / straw wattle deployment on steep slopes to mitigate debris flow hazards before winter storms.

levels.label: High
regions: Mediterranean sclerophyll forests and maquis shrublands
Major petrochemical processing corridors in China, India, and US Gulf Coast
causes: Agricultural land clearing and slash burning following deforestation
Moderate-to-high intensity peat and surface woodland fires
Mid-tier industrial refinery and petrochemical process flaring
Dry-season chaparral and shrubland fires under moderate wind shear
issues: Rapid degradation of regional carbon storage reservoirs
Dense regional smog blankets causing widespread aviation and transport halts
Substantial topsoil heating and localized vegetative canopy kill
Transboundary transport of particulate matter across international boundaries

air_climate: Sustained burning can release extensive carbon dioxide and methane, diminishing the carbon sequestration capacity of forested biomes.
Elevated emissions of NOx and reactive hydrocarbons commonly interact under sunlight to generate regional photochemical smog and ground-level ozone.
Dense PM2.5 smoke plumes can degrade ambient visibility over hundreds of square kilometres.
soil_land: Moderate burn severity can consume protective ground leaf litter, leaving mineral soil exposed to intense raindrop impact and surface rill erosion.
Peat ignition can burn into underlying organic substrate, destabilizing surface topography and root structures.
Industrial particulate settling around refineries can deposit trace hydrocarbons on adjacent agricultural parcels.
water: Runoff carrying ash, nitrates, and dissolved organic carbon can elevate turbidity in municipal surface water intakes.
Increased stream temperatures following canopy loss may stress sensitive cold-water fish taxa and macroinvertebrate communities.
Sediment deposition can reduce reservoir storage capacity and accelerate turbine wear in hydroelectric installations.
snow_ice: Mid-latitude soot deposition can settle onto seasonal alpine snowfields, reducing surface reflectivity and advancing spring melt.
Particulate deposition may reduce glacial albedo in bordering mountainous regions.
wildlife: Canopy and understory mortality can cause significant fragmentation of critical wildlife travel corridors.
Smoke inhalation and rapid flame fronts may cause acute mortality in slow-moving amphibians, reptiles, and ground-dwelling mammals.
Artificial flare illumination and persistent noise can deter sensitive nocturnal mammals.
human_health: Prolonged exposure to regional smoke can increase hospital admissions for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and ischemic heart disease.
Particulate matter can cause widespread eye irritation, bronchitis, and reduced lung capacity among outdoor laborers.
Smoke haze can cause school closures, transport disruptions, and substantial economic losses across agricultural regions.

response_options: Peat and forest management: Rewetting drained peatlands by canal blocking to maintain water table levels and prevent deep subsurface ignition.
Industrial flaring: Installation of low-emission multi-point flare burners, optical flame verification, and vapor recovery systems to reduce slip.
Public health: Timely distribution of N95 respirators, public clean air shelters, and HVAC air filtration advisories during multi-day smoke events.

levels.label: Moderate
regions: Sub-Saharan African savannas and open woodlands
Agricultural cropping belts across Northern India and Southeast Asia
causes: Prescribed early-season savanna burning to reduce late-dry-season fuel loads
Post-harvest crop residue disposal (paddy straw, wheat stubble, sugarcane trash)
Pastoral range burning to stimulate fresh palatable grass growth
Controlled understory broadcast burns in managed commercial timberlands
issues: Recurrent seasonal haze episodes across high-density agricultural basins
Loss of valuable organic soil nitrogen and soil carbon reserves
Cumulative photochemical oxidant generation affecting regional air basins
Displacement of small wildlife from seasonal foraging territories

air_climate: Widespread agricultural and savanna fires can generate seasonal spikes in carbon monoxide, volatile organics, and fine particulates.
Persistent seasonal emissions can react with solar radiation to generate elevated tropospheric ozone levels across downwind agricultural communities.
Smoke plumes commonly settle in valley inversions, causing dense morning haze blankets.
soil_land: Repeated burning can volatilize topsoil nitrogen and sulfur, necessitating higher chemical fertilizer inputs for subsequent crops.
Loss of surface crop stubble can accelerate wind erosion during dry pre-monsoon windy periods.
Surface soil temperatures can temporarily disrupt shallow earthworm and beneficial insect populations.
water: First post-burn runoff can flush dissolved nutrients and loose ash into local canals, ditches, and farm retention ponds.
Temporary nutrient enrichment in shallow waterways can stimulate nuisance filamentous algae growth.
Fine silt transport can increase sedimentation rates in irrigation canals.
snow_ice: Atmospheric transport of carbonaceous aerosols may occasionally reach elevated snowlines in adjacent mountain ranges under favorable wind trajectories.
wildlife: Prescribed burns can temporarily eliminate nesting cover for ground-dwelling birds and rodents.
Fast-moving surface grass fires can occasionally trap small non-volant fauna if escape refugia are insufficient.
Periodic cool-season fires can promote diverse herbaceous vegetation that benefits grazing ungulates over the long term.
human_health: Agricultural smoke can aggravate pediatric asthma and cause recurring allergic conjunctivitis and throat irritation.
Prolonged exposure during seasonal harvesting windows can impair respiratory function in rural farm workers.
Visibility reduction from agricultural haze can elevate highway motor vehicle collision risks in rural transport corridors.

response_options: Residue valorization: Mechanized straw baling for bioenergy pellets, thermal cogeneration, or biochar production to enrich farmland without open-air combustion.
Early dry-season savanna burning: Conducting strategic cool-season burns when grass curing is partial, reducing net carbon emissions and late-season fire severity.
Soil moisture coordination: Utilizing satellite soil moisture products and real-time ventilation index forecasts to schedule prescribed burns on optimal dispersion days.

levels.label: Low or smouldering
regions: Sub-Arctic and boreal peatlands ('zombie' or overwintering fires)
Underground coal seam fires (Jharia basin in India, Ningxia in China, Appalachian basin)
Residual post-front smouldering logs, stump holes, and forest slash piles
causes: Subsurface smouldering propagation through dense organic peat or duff layers
Overwintering 'zombie' combustion surviving beneath snow cover in Arctic peat
Spontaneous combustion or abandoned seam fires in exposed coal seams and mine tailings
Low-temperature flameless smouldering in forestry harvest residues and slash
issues: Incomplete combustion producing elevated toxic emission ratios per megawatt of radiative power
Subsurface spread that can remain undetected by visual observation for months before breaking out into flaming wildfires
Substantial subterranean ground collapse, subsidence, and hazard to personnel
Continuous year-round greenhouse gas emissions independent of seasonal weather

air_climate: Low-temperature smouldering emits disproportionately large quantities of carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH4), and hazardous air pollutants per unit of fuel consumed.
Subsurface combustion commonly releases volatile polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), hydrogen cyanide (HCN), and volatilized heavy metals like mercury.
Smouldering smoke has low thermal buoyancy, hugging the ground in high concentrations and pooling in inhabited lowlands.
soil_land: Subsurface smouldering can consume deep organic soil layers that required centuries or millennia to accumulate.
Underground seam combustion can create subterranean void cavities, triggering severe ground collapse, surface sinkholes, and infrastructural damage.
Smouldering can destroy root systems from within, causing unexpected tree falls across roadways and firelines.
water: Seepage from smouldering coal and peat beds can leach acidic drainage, dissolved organic carbon, and heavy metals directly into groundwater aquifers.
Combustion products can contaminate local springs and pristine headwater wetlands with aromatic compounds.
Permafrost degradation around smouldering sites can alter surface drainage patterns, draining tundra lakes.
snow_ice: Overwintering zombie fires can smoulder beneath seasonal snowpack, transferring heat into permafrost soils and accelerating sub-surface thaw.
Spring breakout of smouldering peat fires directly deposits soot onto melting snowpack, accelerating regional albedo degradation.
wildlife: Destruction of sub-surface burrows, rodent tunnels, and hibernacula can lead to severe mortality of overwintering fauna.
Dense ground-level toxic gas accumulation in hollows can asphyxiate ground-dwelling birds and mammals.
Loss of insulating permafrost moss layers damages unique tundra micro-habitats.
human_health: High concentrations of carbon monoxide and toxic organic vapors pose acute life-threatening inhalation hazards to wildland firefighters and community residents.
Severe burn hazards and risk of traumatic injury from stepping onto concealed subterranean combustion pits and sinkholes.
Long-term exposure to coal seam smoke can cause chronic pneumoconiosis, respiratory illness, and elevated heavy metal body burdens.

response_options: Subsurface thermal monitoring: Deployment of thermal infrared drones and ground temperature probes to map hidden subterranean combustion perimeters.
High-volume soil quenching: Deep soil trenching combined with high-volume water injection using surfactant wetting agents to saturate hydrophobic organic layers.
Mine sealing & smothering: Inert gas injection (nitrogen/CO2) into underground coal voids or covering surface fissures with compact, non-combustible clay overburden.
